questions.q: What is the central "character" (protagonist) of the chapter "वखत खा तक़रीबन ग्यारह इज़्क़्फ़" and how is it introduced in the opening paragraph?
questions.a: The protagonist is Fatehpur Sikri (eqvutks&nM+ks), introduced as India's and the world's most magnificent and awe-inspiring city, where the author's childhood imagination was captivated by tales of its grandeur, ruins, and historical mysteries. A wrong answer (e.g., naming Akbar or the narrator) reveals the student misses the text's personification of the city itself as the central consciousness — a common error when students expect a human protagonist in every narrative.

questions.q: Explain in your own words how the author establishes Fatehpur Sikri's "personality" through the contrast between its past glory and present silence. Use two specific textual details.
questions.a: The city's personality emerges as majestic yet melancholic, proud yet abandoned. Past glory: "बादशाह अकबर ने इसी नगर को अपनी राजधानी बनाया था" (Akbar made this city his capital) and "फतेहपुर सीकरी की शान के किस्से" (tales of its splendor). Present silence: "कोई आहट नहीं," "सन्नाटा," and the narrator hearing only "पत्थरों की आवाज़" (sound of stones). A wrong answer listing facts without interpreting them as *character traits* shows the student treats description as information rather than characterization — they see "what happened" but not "who the city is."

questions.q: Apply the "SHOW, DON'T TELL" principle: Find three instances where the text *shows* Fatehpur Sikri's character through sensory details (sight, sound, touch) rather than directly stating its qualities. Quote the Hindi phrase and name the sense.
questions.a: 1. Sight: "लाल बलुआ पत्थर की दीवारें... धूप में तपती हुई" (red sandstone walls baking in sun) — shows endurance and heat. 2. Sound: "पत्थरों की आवाज़" (sound of stones) / "सन्नाटे में... गूँज" (echo in silence) — shows voice without words. 3. Touch: "दीवारों पर हाथ फेरते ही... इतिहास की धड़कन" (touching walls, feeling history's pulse) — shows tactile connection to past. A wrong answer quoting abstract nouns ("वीरानी," "शान") reveals the student cannot distinguish *evidence* from *interpretation* — a critical gap for board answer-writing where marks require textual proof.

questions.q: Analyze how the narrator's shifting perspectives (childhood imagination → historical research → personal visit → philosophical reflection) build a *layered* portrait of the protagonist. Which perspective contributes most to the city's tragic dignity? Justify.
questions.a: Childhood: mythic grandeur ("कहानियों का शहर"). Historical: political agency ("अकबर की राजधानी," "बुलंद दरवाज़ा"). Personal visit: sensory intimacy ("पत्थर छुए," "सन्नाटा सुना"). Philosophical: universal meaning ("साम्राज्य क्षणभंगुर हैं"). The *personal visit* contributes most to tragic dignity because it grounds the city's greatness in tangible, vulnerable reality — the narrator *touches* the stones that once held power, making the loss physical, not abstract. A wrong answer picking "historical research" shows the student values facts over the text's emotional architecture; they miss that the protagonist's dignity comes from *being felt*, not just *being recorded*.

questions.q: Evaluate this claim: "Fatehpur Sikri is a passive victim of history — things happen *to* it, it does not act." Defend or refute using three textual actions attributed to the city.
questions.a: Refute. The city *acts*: 1. "यह नगर... अकबर को अपनी ओर खींचता है" (the city draws Akbar to itself) — agency in choosing its master. 2. "इसने साम्राज्य का उत्थान और पतन दोनों देखा... और चुपचाप सहा" (it witnessed rise and fall and endured silently) — endurance as active choice. 3. "आज भी यह अपनी कहानी सुनाता है... जो सुनना चाहे" (even today it tells its story to those who listen) — narrative agency in ruins. A wrong answer accepting the claim reveals the student reads only the abandonment, missing the text's consistent personification of the city as a *conscious witness* — a misreading that flattens the protagonist into a backdrop.

questions.q: Create a 4-line "character monologue" in Hindi where Fatehpur Sikri speaks in first person, synthesizing its birth, glory, abandonment, and current voice. Use imagery from the text (red stone, Buland Darwaza, silence, wind).
questions.a:
लाल पत्थर की छाती पर अकबर का सपना बसाया था मैंने,
बुलंद दरवाज़े से आसमान को झुकाया था मैंने।
शहंशाह गए, सेनाएँ गईं, रह गया केवल सन्नाटा,
आज भी हवा से कहता हूँ — "सुनो, मैं अब भी वही हूँ।"
A poor answer using generic ruins imagery ("टूटे महल," "उजाड़") without specific textual anchors (Buland Darwaza, red stone, the narrator's touch) shows the student hasn't internalized the *particular* character the text builds — they default to cliché.
